summary: This is an April 1st humor RFC, so it should not be read as a real specification. It jokes about routers and middleboxes that terminate IP packets, presenting common scenarios of 'wrongful termination' and recommendations for avoiding them. The text plays on legal language about unfair dismissal.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8367 is an April 1st joke that describes packet filtering as “wrongful termination.” It lists common reasons a router may discard packets, while noting that filtering can also serve security purposes.

subtitle: An April 1st RFC treats packet filtering as a case of unfair dismissal.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke frames packet filtering as unfair treatment when network devices discard packets based on their characteristics.
tldr.mechanism: It describes six satirical cases involving packet color, age, origin, length, IP version, and fragmentation flags, then recommends equal treatment of packets.
tldr.outcome: The “Equal Opportunity Device” conclusion is humorous. The RFC also acknowledges that looser packet filtering may compromise security.

today: RFC 8367 is an Informational April 1st document. Its employment-law framing of packet filtering is humorous, and its security section acknowledges that filtering may be needed.

sections.title: Packets and Filtering
sections.content: Routers and middleboxes may discard packets that fail a filtering policy. The RFC notes that filtering can be used for sanity checking, policy enforcement, and security, but says some policies can cause false positives or unnecessary drops. It presents this topic as “wrongful termination” in an April 1st joke.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices sometimes discard packets because of their contents or properties. The RFC jokes about this as if packets were being unfairly fired.

sections.title: Six Satirical Cases
sections.content: The RFC discusses filtering based on color, age (TTL or Hop Limit), source address prefix, length, IP version, and fragmentation flags. It gives examples such as a router dropping IPv6 packets or packets with a More Fragments flag. The employment-law framing turns these filtering cases into jokes about discrimination.
sections.plainLanguage: The six cases concern packet color, age, origin, length, IP version, and flags. The paper gives each one an employment-discrimination name for comic effect.

sections.title: The Limits of the Satire
sections.content: The memo concludes that routers should be “Equal Opportunity Devices” and not discriminate among packets. Its security section immediately notes that a liberal approach to filtering may compromise security. The RFC therefore presents its recommendations in a satirical context rather than as a practical rule to remove filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper jokes that devices should treat every packet equally. It also points out that removing filtering can create security problems.
